title: Search inside a CRM
excerpt: A salesperson searches when the navigation failed. Show matches in their language, and give them a way back to the record they left.
alt: A two-lane road through red rock, with a single car far ahead and a mountain at the end, a route with a visible way onward and back.
caption: A road through red rock, one car, and the way back still in view. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When do salespeople use CRM search?
faqs.answer: They search when the list, the filters, or the first screen failed to put the right record in front of them. Treat search as the recovery path, not as a power-user trophy. The box should be easy to find, and the results should be in the words they use for people, companies, and deals.

faqs.question: What should results show?
faqs.answer: Show the kind of record, the name they would recognize, and one line of context such as the company or the next step. Group or label people, companies, and deals in plain language. A table of every column in the database is a second failure after the navigation already failed.

faqs.question: How do they get back?
faqs.answer: Keep a way back to the record they were on before they searched. Do not replace their place in the product with a results page that forgets it. A back control, or the previous record still available, matters more between calls than a perfect ranking algorithm.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
CRM search UX matters because the salesperson searches when the navigation failed. They are still the person updating a record between calls. They reached for search because the list, the recent items, or your guess of "the next record" was wrong. Show matches in their language, and give them a way back.

Search is a rescue. Design it like one, not like a product launch.

## Navigation already failed

Do not welcome them to search. Do not teach search operators in a modal. They typed a fragment of a name because the account was not where the first screen promised. Every extra step is another second in which the note lives only in their head.

Put the field where a miss sends the hand: the top of the record, the top of the list, the same place every time. A search buried in a command palette they have not learned is a second navigation failure. Command palettes are fine for people who live in the tool. The between-call user is not trying to become a power user before the next ring. They are trying to find Northwind, or "the person named Priya from the warehouse account."

[Nielsen Norman Group](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) describes how quickly people abandon a page that does not show its value, often in 10 to 20 seconds, and how an average time on page hides that early exit. Search results are a page. If the first screenful is a loading skeleton, an ad for advanced filters, or a pile of near-matches with no labels, they will back out and try the list again, or they will give up and write the note in the wrong record. Show something useful immediately: the query they typed, and the closest records, labeled.

Recent records are the other half of rescue. If the navigation failure was "I was just here," recents above the results, or instead of results when the query is empty, will beat a clever index. Empty search should not be a blank sermon about what search can do. It should be the last few records they touched.

## The words they actually type

They type a first name, a misspelled company, a phone fragment, a piece of an email, or the buyer's words ("the candle people") rather than your legal account name. The index has to be kinder than an exact match. A single typo should not produce a smug empty state. Show the close matches, and show what you corrected, in a line they can reject. "Showing results for Northwind." If that guess is wrong, one tap should return to the literal string.

Do not require them to pick a type before they type. "Search in: Deals" as a mandatory scope is how you hide the contact they wanted. Search the things they mix up, people, companies, and deals, and label each hit so the mix is not a muddle. Scope is a refinement after the first results, not a gate.

Phone numbers and emails deserve their own kindness. Ignore formatting. A pasted number with spaces and a stored number with none are the same person. Teams lose half an hour merging duplicates that search itself created by being literal. Be literal in what you display. Be loose in what you match.

Nicknames and former names belong in the same idea if you store them. "Bob" should find "Robert" only when you are confident, and the result should show the name on the record so they know why it appeared. A magic match with no explanation feels like the wrong person. Between calls, the cost of opening the wrong person is a note on the wrong life.

## Matches in their language

Each result needs a type they already say out loud. Person. Company. Deal. Not "Object." Not an icon with no label. The primary line is the name. The secondary line is the disambiguator: the company for a person, the amount and stage for a deal, the city only if you have two companies with the same name.

Highlight the part that matched, so they can see why this row appeared. If it matched a note buried in the record, say "matched in a note" rather than pretending the company name matched. They will open a note match with different expectations. Honor that.

Sort by usefulness, and say if you are doing something surprising. Recent and close matches first. A giant account they never touch should not outrank the person they emailed this morning just because the account's name contains the same syllable. If you boost recency, you do not need a white paper. You need to be consistent enough that they learn the list.

Permissions still apply. A record they cannot open should not pretend to be a normal hit. Show it with the same honesty as a disabled button: the name, and "You can see this exists. Sam owns it." Hiding it entirely makes search look broken, which is the problem that brought them here. Showing the private note inside it is the opposite mistake. The title can be visible. The content stays gated. This is the same sentence as the permission model, repeated where search would otherwise launder a bypass.

## A way back

Remember the record they left. The search page that replaces the whole application, with no path back except the browser's back button, throws away the draft they were in the middle of. Keep the draft. Keep a visible return: "Back to Northwind." If they pick a result, open it, and if it is wrong, returning to the results should be dull and instant, with the query intact.

Do not clear the query on navigation. A cleared query looks like the product forgot them. They will not retype a fiddly name they already fought to spell. Persist it for the session. Clear it when they clear it.

If the result they open is the right one, the first screen of that record takes over, with its one action. Search should not strand them on a preview that cannot take the note. Previews are how demos look fast and real work gets slower. Open the record. Put the cursor in the note. They searched in order to write.

A way back also means a way to undo a bad merge or a bad open. If they started a note on the result and then realized it was the other Priya, let them move the draft. Do not make them copy, cancel, search again, and paste. That flow is how notes get split across two people who share a first name.

## The empty and the too-full

Empty, after a real query, should be humble. "No people, companies, or deals match 'Nortwind'." Offer the spelling you suspect, and offer to create a person only if creating a person is truly their job in this gap. Creating a duplicate because search failed is a common scar in CRMs. Bias toward finding. Make creation a deliberate second step with the company attached, not a big button that fires when the list is empty.

Too-full is the other failure. A query of "a" should not render the entire database in a scrolling monument. Ask for another letter, or show recents, rather than pretending you have ranked tens of thousands of useful hits. Performance is part of the rescue. A search that takes longer than the gap is a navigation failure with a spinner.

Show a count only if it helps them decide to refine. "200 deals" with no way to narrow by their own book is a brag. "12 in your accounts" is a tool. Default the scope to what they can act on, and let them widen to the whole company when the record is someone else's. Widening should be obvious. A silent default that hides the rest of the company will be called a bug, just like a hidden button.

## What not to rank first

Do not rank a help article above the account. They are inside the product, mid-job. Documentation in the same list as people is a category error. If you must offer help, put it in a different place, visually distinct, and only when the query looks like a question rather than a name.

Do not rank a create-new action above the matches. The number of duplicate companies in a typical CRM is the history of that mistake. Matches first. Create last, labeled with the exact name they typed so they can see they are about to mint "Nortwind" and not "Northwind."

Do not interleave marketing modules, dashboards, and settings into the same results as the book of business. Settings search can exist. It should not kidnap a person search. The salesperson did not mean "notification preferences" when they typed a buyer's name. If your search is a single omnibox, separate the sections with labels strong enough to skip. People. Companies. Deals. Then, far away, the rest of the product.

Filters that require a manual refresh, or that reset when they return from a record, are the navigation failure coming back for a second pass. Keep the filter next to the query. Make it a word they use, "mine" and "open," not a query-language souvenir.

## Test it with the name they mumbled

Take a real call recording, or a fair reconstruction, and use only the words that were said. First name. Wrong spelling. Company nickname. Time the path from that fragment to a saved note on the right record, including the way back if the first hit is wrong. If it takes more than the gap, search is still a second product they have to learn. Cut operators, cut mandatory scopes, cut the preview pane, until the path is a type, a tap, and a note.

Do this with a rep's account, not an admin's. Admin search that sees everything will pass a test the rep will fail. The rep's empty state is the one that ships.

The product area they reach for when the day is quieter, and something structural has to change, is not search. [Settings in a CRM](/blog/settings-in-a-crm) is the next piece, because settings are a cabinet, not a second product, and most of them should stay out of the between-call path entirely.

[Selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) is where you can see how Hanabi handles a product surface that has to be scanned quickly: one hierarchy, and a way through.
